full_judgment:
Plaintiffs are the appellants in FMA No. 18 of 1984 while defendant Nos. 1& 2 are the appellants in FMA No. 21 of 1984. 

 2. The suit was brought to enforce specific performance of a contract alleged to have been made by defendant No. 1 for sale of the disputed property which consists of 0.625 acre of land with structures thereon situated within the town of Bogra. At the institution of the suit the plaintiffs filed an application praying for temporary injunction restraining defendant Nos. 1.3 from dispossessing the plaintiffs from the disputed property. It was alleged in the application that the disputed land belonged to defendant No. 1. She used to run business thereon with the help of her son defendant No. 2. During the War of Liberation the entire shop was looted away and she took shelter at Saidpur for safety of her life. The disputed property remained vacant. Plaintiff No, 4 took the vacant land in his possession and constructed new structures thereon at a cost of Tk. 1,00,000. During the last part of 1976 defendant Nos. 1 & 2 came back to Bogra and they proposed to sell the property to the plaintiffs who agreed to purchase the same at a consideration of Tk. 3,50,000. Owing to certain technical difficulties the plaintiffs wanted to have the baina-nama executed in favour of their relations namely, proforma defendant Nos. 4-9. Accordingly, defendant No. 1 executed a bainanama on receipt of a sum of Tk. 50,000 in cash and 50,000 by pay order from the plaintiffs as earnest money and the plaintiffs have since been in possession of the property on the basis of the said bainanama. In spite of repeated demands for the requisite kabala, defendant No. 1 did execute and register the kabala in favour of the plaintiffs as agreed. It was further alleged that defendants Nos. 1 & 2 were trying to dispossess the plaintiffs from the disputed property with the help of defendant No. 3 and unless the said defendants were restrained by an order of injunction from evicting and or dispossessing the plaintiffs from the disputed property they would suffer an irreparable loss and injuries. 

 4. After the due service of notice defendant No. 1 appeared and opposed the application by filing a written objection. She denied to have made any contract either with the plaintiffs or with the proforma defendant Nos. 4-9. She asserted that she was an inhabitant Kakinara within the district of 24 Parganas in West Bengal. She got the disputed property by exchange dated 22-6-66 and since then she had been in possession of the same. During the War of Liberation she fled away to Saidpur. Taking advantage of her absence some interested per-sons took possession of the property and managed to get the same declared as abandoned property. She objected but failed to obtain any relief from the district authorities. She subsequently made a representation to the Government and the Government passed an order on 16.4.83 for release of the property in her favour. She asserted that the plaintiffs have brought the suit in collusion with proforma defendant Nos. 4-9 only to grab the property. 

 5. On consideration of the respective cases of the parties the learned Sub-ordinate Judge took the view that the plain-tiffs had a good prima facie case and that they were entitled to injunction against defendant Nos. 1& 2. So far as the plaintiffs' prayer for injunction against the Government-defendant No. 3 is concerned, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge formed an opinion that no ad-interim order for maintenance of status quo could be given without hearing the Government under Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 and, as such, the interim order for maintenance of status quo should not be allowed to exist. Accordingly, by an order dated 27-9-84, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge made the ad-interim order of status quo absolute against defendant Nos. 1 & 2 and rejected the prayer of the plaintiffs as regards defendant No. 3. 

 6. Against the refusal of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge to grant temporary injunction against defendant No. 3, the plaintiffs have filed FMA No. 18 of 1984 while defendant Nos. 1& 2 filed FMA No. 21 of 1984 against the order so far as it related to them. 

 7. Mr Ansar Ali, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants in FMA No. 21 of 1984, mainly urged that the plaintiffs have failed to make out a prima facie case for injunction and as such the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was wrong in passing an order of status quo against the defendant Nos. 1 & 2. Mr SS Haldar, learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondents, on the other hand, supports the order of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge. He submits that regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was justified in holding that the plaintiffs have a good prima facie case. 

 8. It is seen that the plaintiffs have based their claim on a bainanama dated 27-1-77 purporting to have been executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of proforma defendant Nos. 4.9. It is alleged by the plaintiffs that defendant No. 1 entered into the contract with the plaintiffs for sale of the property but owing to some technical difficulties they got the agreement executed in favour of the proforma defendant Nos. 4-9 who are their relations. It is also alleged that in pursuance of the contract defendant No. 1 received Tk. 50,000 in cash and Tk. 50,000 by pay order from the plaintiffs as earnest money out of the total consideration of Tk. 3,50,000 and made over possession of the property to the plaintiffs and they are in possession of the disputed property. In the written objection filed by the defendant No. 1 she has denied to have entered into any contract either with the plaintiffs or with the proforma defendant Nos. 4-9. She has, however, quoted a letter dated 10-9-82 written by her in reply to a notice dated 2-9-82 issued by one Mr. Md. Anisur Rahman, Advocate demanding a kabala in pursuance of a bainanama dated 27-1-77. The contents of the letter are reproduced below:— 

 9. The defendant No. 1 appears to have taken a stand in the said letter that she and her son put signatures and thumb impression on a deed of agreement in respect of the disputed property and received a pay order for Tk. 50,000 under coercion. It is also noticed from the materials placed before us that proforma defendant Nos. 4-9 who are alleged by the plaintiffs to be their relations appeared in the suit and they filed a petition of compromise admitting the claim of the plaintiffs. 

 10. So far as the possession of the property is concerned the plaintiffs claim that they are in possession. Defendant No. 1 on the other hand, admits in her written objection that since the War of Liberation they have not been in possession of the property but she has asserted that taking advantage of her absence some interested persons took possession of the property. She has not mentioned who are the said interested persons. At the instance of the plaintiffs a local inspection was held and the learned Advocate Commissioner appears to have submitted a report which shows that the property is in possession of the plaintiffs. 

 11. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the opinion that the plaintiffs have been able to make out a good prima facie case for injunction and the learned Sub-ordinate Judge committed no illegality in arriving at a finding to that effect. The balance of convenience and inconvenience is also in favour of the plaintiffs. So we do not find any substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants and the appeal must, therefore, fail. 

 12. Mr SS Haldar, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff appellants in FMA No. 18 of 1984 assailed the order of refusal of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge to grant injunction against the Government on the ground that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge misread the provision of Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 and thus committed a substantial error in refusing to grant injunction in the facts and circumstances of the case. According to him, no public work or programme of the Government is likely to be effected if an injunction is granted against the Government appears to have entered appearance in the case but did not file any written objection to the prayer of the plaintiffs for injunction. Mr. Quazi Akhtar Hosain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appeared in this appeal in support of the order of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge but there being no written objection filed by them before tire learned Sub-ordinate Judge, the latter finds it difficult to contend that if any order for maintenance of status quo or injunction is granted the same shall have the edict of prejudicing any development work of the Government. 

 14. It seems clear from the above discussion that under Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 service of notice upon the Government is one of the pre-requisites for exercise of the power of granting injunction against the Government to the instant case the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has taken the view that the ad-interim order of status quo is illegal as the same was Passed without service of notice upon the Government and as the interim order is illegal, no order for temporary injunction can be made. It is true that the ad-interim order is illegal being violative of Martial Law Order No. 40 of 1982 but will that preclude the Court from granting an order of temporary injunction if the plaintiffs are otherwise entitled thereto? Our answer will be 'No'. Prayers for temporary and ad-interim injunction are distinct and separate and the exercise of the power of granting temporary injunction is not defendant on the grant of an ad-interim order. Non-compliance with the provision in granting an ad-interim order an not, therefore, deprive a party to have a relief by way of temporary injunction if the condition of Martial Law Order No. 40 are fulfilled and the party is otherwise entitled to the same, In our opinion, therefore, the view taken by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge does not appear to be correct. It is noticed that the Government had passed an order for release of the from the list of abandoned property in favour of defendant No. 1. Now what is left for the Government is to make over possession of the property to her if the Government is in possession thereof at all. Such an act, if restrained, will not have the effect of interfering with any public work or development plan or programme of the Government. We have already found that the plaintiffs have made out a prima facie case for injunction. We have also found that a reasonable notice of the application for injunction was given to the Government and that an order for maintenance of status quo will not prejudicially affect any development work of the Government, Our considered opinion, therefore, is that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in not granting the prayer of the plaintiffs against the defendant No. 3, We submission of the learned Advocate for the appellants his foundation. The appeal must succeed.
